excerpt: Nolan's 181-minute epic finally gives his maximalism a subject worthy of it, and Cillian Murphy gives the performance of his career.
markdown:
Christopher Nolan has spent his career filming clever men outrunning consequences, but Oppenheimer is the first time the consequences catch up — and the first time his maximalism feels fully justified. Across 181 minutes, Nolan compresses J. Robert Oppenheimer's stewardship of the atomic bomb during World War II into a procedural, a ghost story, and a political knife fight stacked inside one another. Cillian Murphy holds the whole unstable reaction together with the most withholding performance of his career. I found it exhausting in the best possible way: the rare biopic that treats history as a live wire instead of a museum piece.

## What works

- **Murphy's negative space.** His Oppenheimer talks softly and listens horribly well. Nolan keeps pushing the camera into his eyes until you feel a man doing arithmetic that ends in ash. There is no vanity in it, no showcase weeping — just a brilliant administrator realizing, too late, what he administered. It is the kind of lead performance that reorganizes the entire film around itself.
- **The Strauss axis.** Robert Downey Jr. plays Lewis Strauss as wounded vanity curdling into menace, and his interrogation-room sparring with Murphy gives the back half its bitter charge. Matt Damon lends Leslie Groves a blustering warmth, while Emily Blunt and Florence Pugh squeeze entire marriages and affairs into a handful of scenes each.
- **Pressure-chamber craft.** For a three-hour film built from meetings and hearings, the cutting rarely idles. Committee rooms throb like engine rooms, and the dread compounds rather than dissipates — every breakthrough lands with a shadow attached. That a film this talky earned a $952 million worldwide gross tells you the tension transferred to audiences.

## What doesn't

The middle hour sags under its own apparatus. Figures like Ernest Lawrence arrive, deliver exposition, and evaporate, while Jean Tatlock's storyline compresses to shorthand — which undersells both Pugh and the tragedy. Nolan's allergy to stillness occasionally smothers confrontations that needed room to breathe, and the dialogue sometimes announces themes the images already delivered. Trust the stare, Christopher.

## Verdict

Oppenheimer is Nolan's most disciplined spectacle: a biopic engineered like a thriller that lingers like a warning. It demands commitment — the runtime is real, the density is real — but Murphy's hollowed-out center holds it upright, and the final movement lands with genuine moral force. See it loud, then sit with it in silence after.

**Rating: 9/10**

excerpt: Bong Joon Ho's 133-minute class thriller remains the decade's most precisely engineered film — a caper, a farce, and a tragedy in one skin.
markdown:
Few films redraw themselves in your memory the way Parasite does. Bong Joon Ho's 133-minute braid of comedy, thriller, and drama opens like a con-artist caper — Ki-taek's unemployed family insinuating itself, member by member, into the service of the wealthy, glamorous Parks — and then metastasizes into something closer to a trap snapping shut. I laughed through the first hour and sat in rigid silence for the last twenty minutes, which is exactly the ratio Bong intended. It is the most precisely engineered film of its decade, and the engineering stays invisible right up until it cuts you.

## What works

- **The vertical screenplay.** Bong maps class onto physical space — who lives above whom, who climbs, who descends — and every scheme the Kim family runs doubles as a tour of that geography. Song Kang-ho anchors it all as Ki-taek with hangdog cunning, while Choi Woo-shik and Park So-dam play the sibling con with the easy rhythm of people who have rehearsed survival their whole lives.
- **Tone as a weapon.** The film glides from farce to menace without a visible gear change; a single sequence can pivot on one line reading. Lee Sun-kyun and Cho Yeo-jeong play the Parks not as villains but as weather — oblivious, well-meaning, structurally unreachable — which makes the eventual collision hurt far more than any mustache-twirling could.
- **An ending that recontextualizes.** When the unexpected incident the premise promises finally detonates, it does not merely escalate the story — it rewrites everything that came before it. Few thrillers reward rewatches; Parasite improves on the second viewing, because you realize how openly Bong showed his hand all along.

## What doesn't

If there is a demerit, it is that one late revelation leans on coincidence to assemble its players, and subtitle readers will inevitably miss a blink-and-miss visual gag or two on first viewing. The final movement also deliberately withholds catharsis, which some viewers will read as coldness. I read it as honesty — and a $257.6 million worldwide gross suggests the world agreed to meet it halfway.

## Verdict

Parasite is a heist movie, a farce, and a tragedy sharing one skin, and Bong sheds each layer at exactly the right moment. Flawless structure, lethal tonal control, and an ending that still stings years later. This is the essential thriller of its era.

**Rating: 9.5/10**

excerpt: Cameron's 194-minute epic disarmed my irony within the hour — the craft is total, the leads carry it, and the sinking still devastates.
markdown:
It is fashionable to be superior about Titanic, and I arrived at my rewatch armed with irony. James Cameron's 194-minute romance-disaster epic disarmed me within the hour. The framing device — 101-year-old Rose DeWitt Bukater recounting her voyage 84 years later — should feel creaky, and instead it works like a slow tide. By the time young Rose boards with her mother and fiancé while Jack Dawson and Fabrizio De Rossi celebrate their third-class tickets, the film has you, and it never really lets go. Sentiment this naked only works with craft this total, and Cameron brings the craft.

## What works

- **The two-film structure.** Cameron essentially bolts a swooning class romance onto a disaster procedural, and each half powers the other — the love story gives the sinking its faces, the sinking gives the love story its clock. The 194 minutes justify themselves; the first two hours are foreplay for devastation, and the patience pays off brutally.
- **The leads.** Leonardo DiCaprio's Jack is all kinetic charm, Kate Winslet's Rose a slow detonation of defiance, and their chemistry does the heavy lifting the dialogue occasionally cannot. Around them, Billy Zane commits to magnificent bastardy as Cal Hockley, Kathy Bates steals every deck she walks as Molly Brown, and Gloria Stuart's elder Rose gives the memory its ache.
- **Physical conviction.** The ship feels present in a way modern green-screen epics rarely achieve — weight, water, and panic rendered at full scale. Cameron shoots the sinking as engineering in reverse, and the set-pieces remain genuinely harrowing decades on. A $2.264 billion worldwide gross is no accident; it is what happens when spectacle serves feeling.

## What doesn't

The dialogue creaks — some exchanges between Jack and Rose read like greeting cards, and Cal's villainy has no shading whatsoever. The framing device also pauses the momentum exactly when you least want pausing, and the middle stretch leans hard on montages of rich people being awful. And yes, the door discourse persists; the film's answer is emotional rather than logistical, and you either accept that or you don't.

## Verdict

Titanic is the blockbuster as grand opera: shameless, overwhelming, and built to last. Mock the dialogue all you want — you will still cry when the band plays on. Few films commit this completely to feeling, and fewer still earn it.

**Rating: 8.5/10**

excerpt: Peele's 104-minute horror-thriller remains a precision instrument — social dread curdling into nightmare, with Kaluuya holding every frame.
markdown:
Horror rarely feels this controlled. Jordan Peele's 104-minute braid of mystery, thriller, and horror starts from a deceptively small premise — Chris accompanying his girlfriend Rose upstate to meet her parents — and plays its first half as pure social dread. The overly accommodating smiles, the comments that land half an inch wrong, the feeling of being studied: I felt my shoulders climbing toward my ears long before anything explicitly terrifying happened. That is the film's signature trick. The scares are real, but the unease is the masterpiece, and Peele conducts both like he has been doing it for decades.

## What works

- **Dread by accumulation.** Peele understands that horror lives in the edit and the sound mix as much as in any reveal. Glances linger a beat too long, pleasantries curdle mid-sentence, and the sterile brightness of the house becomes oppressive. By the time the weekend's disturbing discoveries start compounding, your nerves are already gone — the film spent an hour quietly taking them.
- **Kaluuya's face.** Daniel Kaluuya plays Chris as a man performing calm while his instincts scream, and his reactive acting is the film's grounding wire — every flicker of doubt or forced politeness registers. Allison Williams matches him as Rose with a performance that weaponizes charm, while Catherine Keener and Bradley Whitford radiate the specific menace of hospitality with conditions.
- **The payoff lands clean.** When the truth Chris could never have imagined finally surfaces, it retroactively sharpens every awkward exchange that preceded it. The final act converts all that stored tension into propulsive, cathartic horror without betraying the setup. A $255.4 million worldwide gross on a lean budget proved precision beats excess.

## What doesn't

The third act explains its machinery a touch more than necessary — one sequence of villainous exposition tells us what the images had already made clear. A couple of comic-relief beats release pressure the film worked hard to build, and viewers who poke at the logistics afterward will find threads worth pulling. None of it dents the experience in the moment, but the sheen dulls slightly on repeat viewings.

## Verdict

Get Out is the rare horror debut that plays like the work of a veteran: socially observant, technically exact, and genuinely frightening. It earns its place in the genre canon one queasy smile at a time. See it with an audience that gasps.

**Rating: 9/10**

excerpt: DaCosta's 109-minute chapter pairs Fiennes' unsettling Kelson with feral cult menace — grim, tactile horror that mostly delivers.
markdown:
There is a particular chill that only franchise horror can produce — the dread of returning to a ruined world and finding it worse. Nia DaCosta's 109-minute entry in the 28 Years Later saga, subtitled The Bone Temple, centers on two collisions: Dr. Kelson's shocking new relationship, with consequences that could change the world as its survivors know it, and Spike's encounter with Jimmy Crystal turning into an inescapable nightmare. I walked in braced for a holding-pattern sequel and found something stranger and more tactile: folk dread grafted onto sprinting, snarling survival horror.

## What works

- **Fiennes goes feral-elegant.** Ralph Fiennes plays Dr. Kelson as a man who has adapted past the point of recognition — courteous one moment, feral the next — and his scenes carry a queasy charge the film wisely builds around. Alfie Williams gives Spike a raw, reactive fear that keeps the stakes human-scaled, while Jack O'Connell's Sir Jimmy Crystal radiates the specific terror of charisma gone rotten.
- **Tactile craft.** DaCosta shoots the horror close and wet: breath, mud, teeth. The 109-minute runtime wastes little, and the set-pieces favor geography you can follow over chaos you merely survive. The cult's pageantry — robes, ritual, bone — gives the scares a visual identity distinct from the saga's earlier chapters.
- **Dread with ideas.** Beneath the viscera, the film keeps probing what survival costs and who gets to define community after the end of the world. Kelson's storyline flirts with genuinely provocative questions about adaptation versus humanity, and the horror lands harder for carrying that weight.

## What doesn't

The middle stretch sags between set-pieces, with connective tissue that feels more functional than inspired — characters travel because the plot requires arrival. A few of the cult mechanics blur on first viewing, and the ending plays more as table-setting for the next chapter than as a self-contained gut punch. The $58.5 million worldwide gross suggests audiences showed up curious rather than converted.

## Verdict

The Bone Temple is a grim, tactile middle chapter that mostly justifies itself: strong lead performances, distinctive folk-horror texture, and enough ideas to lift it above franchise filler. It does not reach the saga's highest peaks, but it holds its nerve. Horror completists should not skip it.

**Rating: 7/10**

excerpt: Coogler's 138-minute horror epic pairs Jordan's commanding twin turn with a ferocious ensemble and a blood-soaked final act.
markdown:
Ryan Coogler makes scale feel personal, and Sinners is his boldest swing at that trick. Across 138 minutes of horror, action, and thriller, twin brothers return to their hometown to start over, only to find an even greater evil waiting to welcome them back. That is the whole engine, and it roars. I expected a genre exercise from a prestige director slumming it; what I got was a sweaty, full-blooded nightmare with blockbuster muscle and something real gnawing underneath. The $371.4 million worldwide gross says audiences felt the bite too.

## What works

- **Jordan squared.** Michael B. Jordan carries the twin-brother premise as Smoke and Stack with genuinely differentiated presence — posture, temper, humor — and the film is smart enough to let the brothers' bond do the emotional heavy lifting before the horror closes in. It is a star turn times two, and he never coasts on the gimmick.
- **Ensemble with teeth.** Hailee Steinfeld brings a sharp, defiant edge as Mary, Miles Caton gives Sammie Moore a live-wire vulnerability, and Jack O'Connell's Remmick oozes the kind of villainous charm that makes evil feel like an invitation. Wunmi Mosaku and Jayme Lawson round out a company with no weak links — every face on screen feels cast with intent.
- **Ferocious craft.** Coogler stages the horror with propulsive, physical clarity: the camera moves like it is hunting, the sound mix hits like weather, and the final act unleashes carnage that feels earned rather than obligatory. The 138 minutes fly by because every sequence tightens the noose another notch.

## What doesn't

The first act takes its time assembling the board — necessary, but viewers hungry for horror may fidget before the evil fully announces itself. A few character motivations blur once the blood starts flowing, with survival logic occasionally bending to serve the set-piece. And the mythology of the threat stays deliberately thin, which gives the scares mystery but leaves lore-hungry viewers wanting another reel.

## Verdict

Sinners is a big, bloody, confident genre film from a director operating at full power — anchored by Jordan's double turn and an ensemble that never blinks. It does not reinvent horror, but it reminds you why the ritual works. See it loud, with a crowd.

**Rating: 8.5/10**
